parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by the binding energy of a nucleus.

markscheme_points.text: energy required to separate (all) the nucleons (in the nucleus)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what holds protons and neutrons together in a tiny nucleus - what would you have to do to pull them all apart?
Hint 2: For a full definition, be precise about how far apart the separated nucleons must be so they no longer attract each other.
parts.proper_answer: The binding energy is the energy required to separate all the nucleons in the nucleus to infinity.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What binding really means**
Think of the nucleus as tightly glued together by the strong nuclear force. The nucleons are in a low-energy, stable arrangement. To break it up completely you must do work on it to pull every proton and neutron away from all the others.

Step 2: **Why infinity matters**
As long as nucleons are close they still attract. Only when they are infinitely far apart is the attraction zero and they are fully free. So the definition is: $$ \text{binding energy = energy needed to separate all nucleons to infinity} $$

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Table 9.1 shows the masses of two sub-atomic particles and a polonium-212 ($^{212}_{84}\text{Po}$) nucleus.

Table 9.1

|  | $\text{mass/u}$ |
| proton | 1.007276 |
| neutron | 1.008665 |
| polonium-212 nucleus | 211.942749 |

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: the mass defect $\Delta m$, in kg
hints: Hint 1: Start from the symbol $^{212}_{84}\text{Po}$ - how many protons does 84 tell you, and how many neutrons are left from 212 total nucleons?
Hint 2: Compare the total mass of all those separate protons and neutrons with the actual mass of the bound nucleus - which is larger and why?
Hint 3: Remember to first find the difference in u, then convert to kg using $1\text{ u} = 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Count the separate nucleons**
For $^{212}_{84}\text{Po}$, proton number $Z = 84$ and nucleon number $A = 212$. So number of neutrons $= A - Z = 212 - 84 = 128$. The mass if all were separate is: $$ m_{separate} = 84m_p + 128m_n $$

Step 2: **Find mass defect in u**
Mass defect is separate mass minus bound mass: $$ \Delta m = [(84 \times 1.007276) + (128 \times 1.008665)] - 211.942749 $$ $$ \Delta m = 213.720384 - 211.942749 = 1.778\text{ u (approx)} $$ The bound nucleus is lighter because some mass was converted to binding energy when it formed.

Step 3: **Convert u to kg**
$$ \Delta m = 1.778 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg} $$ $$ \Delta m = 2.95 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg} $$ Keep 3 s.f. to match the data.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall how a small loss of mass when nucleons bind is related to the energy that holds them together.
Hint 2: Check you use the $\Delta m$ in kg from (b)(i) and $c = 3.00 \times 10^8\text{ m s}^{-1}$, giving energy in joules.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link mass defect to energy**
Einstein tells us mass and energy are equivalent. The binding energy is the energy equivalent of the mass defect: $$ E = \Delta m c^2 $$ You must use $\Delta m$ in kg, not in u, to get joules.

Step 2: **Substitute numbers**
$$ E = (2.95 \times 10^{-27}) \times (3.00 \times 10^8)^2 $$ $$ E = 2.66 \times 10^{-10}\text{ J} $$ This is the energy that would be needed to split this one nucleus completely.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: To compare nuclei of different sizes fairly, think how you would share the total binding energy equally among all 212 nucleons.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Divide by total nucleons**
Binding energy per nucleon $= \frac{\text{total binding energy}}{A}$: $$ = \frac{2.66 \times 10^{-10}}{212} = 1.25 \times 10^{-12}\text{ J} $$ A larger value means a more stable nucleus.

parts.label: (c)(i)

markscheme_points.text: line rising to a single peak that is to the left of the '9' in the Fig. 9.1 label and
steep positive gradient on the left of the peak and shallow negative gradient

hints: Hint 1: Recall the famous shape - it climbs very fast for light nuclei, reaches a maximum for medium nuclei around iron, then slowly falls for heavy nuclei.
Hint 2: Think about the slopes - is the rise on the left steep or gentle compared with the fall on the right?
parts.proper_answer: Curve starts low at $A=1$, rises steeply to a peak at $A \approx 50$ to $60$, then falls gradually towards $A=250$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the general shape**
You are sketching one of the most important graphs in physics. Start near the origin, rise very steeply for small $A$ as light nuclei fuse to become more stable.

Step 2: **Peak then gentle fall**
Reach a single broad maximum well to the left of centre, around $A = 56$ for iron, which is the most stable. Then slope down gently to the right toward $A = 250$. The left gradient is much steeper than the right negative gradient. No values on the y-axis are needed, only the shape.

hints: Hint 1: Polonium-212 is very heavy with $A = 212$ - where is 212 on your $A$-axis from 1 to 250, and on which side of the peak is it?
parts.proper_answer: X marked on the descending right-hand part of the curve at $A = 212$, close to the 250 end.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Locate A = 212**
Find 212 on the horizontal axis - it is about 85 percent of the way to 250, far to the right of the peak. Mark X on your curve line there, on the slowly falling section where heavy unstable nuclei sit.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text:
Polonium-212 is radioactive and undergoes alpha-decay.

Suggest and explain, with reference to Fig. 9.1, why the alpha-decay of polonium-212 results in a release of energy.

markscheme_points.text: nucleus formed (as a result of the decay) has a lower nucleon number
(nucleus formed has a) greater binding energy per nucleon

hints: Hint 1: Alpha decay ejects 4 nucleons - what happens to the nucleon number $A$ of the daughter nucleus and which way does it move on Fig. 9.1?
Hint 2: If the new nucleus is higher up the curve, what does that say about its binding energy per nucleon and the total energy released?
parts.proper_answer: Alpha decay reduces the nucleon number, moving leftwards up the curve to greater binding energy per nucleon. The more tightly bound product means energy is released.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Move to higher stability**
Alpha decay: $^{212}\text{Po}$ emits a helium-4 nucleus, so the daughter has $A = 208$. On Fig. 9.1 this is a small move to the left, back up the gentle slope toward the peak.

Step 2: **Why energy comes out**
Higher on the curve means greater binding energy per nucleon, so the daughter plus alpha particle are more tightly bound in total than the parent. The increase in binding comes from a decrease in mass, and the difference is released as kinetic energy of the decay products: $$ \text{lower } A \rightarrow \text{ higher BE per nucleon } \rightarrow \text{ energy released} $$
